changes.text: For Europe draws from thence nothing of solid use; materials to supply luxury, and only perishable commodities, and sends thither gold and silver, which is there buried and never returns. I have good grounds to think, that the silver and gold brought from America, the gold dust brought from Africa, and the silver produced from the European mines, in the 200 years last past, has not amounted to less, in the whole, than 800 millions. There is no appearance of this immense sum in any country of Europe. … The English and Dutch, which together are not 1/10th part of Europe, enjoy this traffic almost without any rivalship; and if it be a burthen, it lies not upon the one, but on the other 9 parts, so that if the East-India trade carry out the gold and silver from this side of the world, it is truly and properly, at the cost and expence of France, Germany, Spain, and the northern kingdoms, who have little or no opportunities of trading thither.

decisions.note: Compared with Avalon's text of An Essay on the East-India Trade ('by Charles D'Avenant, 1697', addressed to the Marquis of Normanby). All words match. changes.translation: Translated by Thomas Nugent (1750), revised by J. V. Prichard; The Spirit of Laws, G. Bell & Sons, London, 1914 (as reproduced by the Constitution Society)
changes.text: Gold and silver are either a fictitious or a representative wealth. The representative signs of wealth are extremely durable, and, in their own nature, but little subject to decay. But the more they are multiplied, the more they lose their value, because the fewer are the things which they represent. The Spaniards, after the conquest of Mexico and Peru, abandoned their natural riches, in pursuit of a representative wealth which daily degraded itself. … However, it was not long before the specie of Europe was doubled; this appeared from the price of commodities, which everywhere was doubled. … The king of Spain, who receives great sums from his custom-house at Cadiz, is in this respect only a rich individual in a state extremely poor.

decisions.note: Compared with constitution.org book 21, chapter 22 'Of the Riches which Spain drew from America' (the heading is right). The site's title page says the text is Nugent's translation as revised by J. V. Prichard, 'based on a public domain edition published in 1914 by G. Bell & Sons, Ltd., London'. The old credit's '1900' is not supported, so the credit was corrected. The first '…' marked only a paragraph break and was removed. The other cuts (on the Indians not knowing mercury; ~900 words of the doubling argument) keep the meaning. Role refined: Montesquieu had sold his office as président à mortier of the Parlement of Bordeaux in 1726, so in 1748 he was a former magistrate. Year 1748 (first edition, Geneva) is right.

Compared with Avalon's Discourses upon Trade (London: Tho. Basset, 1691), 'A Discourse of Coyned Money' and its conclusion. The three pieces are verbatim. They are joined by long cuts (~2,100 and ~1,300 words) but each piece states North's own view and none reverses it. The last piece is his concluding 'uniform Sentiment' that laws hampering trade do not make a people rich. Role is right: a Levant (Turkey) merchant at Smyrna and Constantinople, knighted 1683, later a commissioner of customs and of the Treasury, all before 1691.

changes.text: The king my lord and father (may he rest in peace!) by various decrees prohibited trade and commerce of the Western Indias with the Philipinas Islands and China generally, to obviate the loss that resulted therefrom to these kingdoms and to their trade and commerce. … Although it has been ordered by other decrees at various times that these should be observed and complied with, I have been informed that this has not been done, and that the quantity allowed has been and is being greatly exceeded in the amount taken each year, with the knowledge and permission of my viceroys, audiencias, and governors—goods to the extent of more than two millions of ducats being registered and openly sent, besides what is secretly shipped. All this money finally makes it [sic] way into infidel kingdoms, whereby their power is increased; and from this have resulted great losses to our exchequer and to the commerce of these kingdoms with the Western Indias. … I have decided that for the present the trade and commerce of the said Philipinas Islands with Nueva España should be maintained according to the ordinances.

changes.text: Be it enacted by the King’s most excellent majesty, … That from and after the first day of December one thousand six hundred and sixty, and from thenceforward, no goods or commodities whatsoever shall be imported into or exported out of any lands, islands, plantations or territories to his Majesty belonging or in his possession, … in Asia, Africa, or America, in any other ship or ships, vessel or vessels whatsoever, but in such ships or vessels as do truly and without fraud belong only to the people of England or Ireland, … and all governors of the said lands, islands, plantations or territories, and every of them, are hereby strictly required and commanded, and all who hereafter shall be governors of any such islands, plantations or territories, by his Majesty, his heirs and successors, shall before their entrance into their government take a solemn oath, to do their utmost, that every the aforementioned clauses, and all the matters and things therein contained, shall be punctually and bona fide observed according to the true intent and meaning thereof.

changes.sourceLine: Thomas Mun, London merchant and director of the English East India Company, England's Treasure by Forraign Trade, chapter 2, "The means to enrich the Kingdom, and to encrease our Treasure", written c. 1630, published 1664 (adapted)
changes.original: Although a Kingdom may be enriched by gifts received, or by purchase taken from some other Nations, yet these are things uncertain and of small consideration when they happen. … The ordinary means therefore to encrease our wealth and treasure is by Forraign Trade, wherein wee must ever observe this rule; to sell more to strangers yearly than wee consume of theirs in value. For suppose that when this Kingdom is pletifully served with the Cloth, Lead, Tinn, Iron, Fish and other native commodities, we doe yearly export the overplus to forraign Countries to the value of twenty two hundred thousand pounds; by which means we are enabled beyond the Seas to buy and bring in forraign wares for our use and Consumption, to the value of twenty hundred thousand pounds; By this order duly kept in our trading, we may rest assured that this order duly kept in our trading, we may rest assured that the Kingdom shall be enriched yearly two hundred thousand pounds, which must be brought to us in so much Treasure; because that part of our stock which is not returned to us in wares must necessarily be brought home in treasure.

decisions.note: Checked against the scan behind the Wikisource transcription (Ashley's Economic Classics reprint of the 1664 text, Commons djvu p. 7, image viewed). changes.text: And we find by experience, that without the common help, assistance, and interposition of a General Company, the people designed from hence for those parts cannot be profitably protected and mantained in their great risque from pirates, extortion and otherwise, which will happen in so very long a voyage. … That, moreover, the aforesaid Company may, in our name and authority, within the limits herein before prescribed, … make contracts, engagements and alliances with the princes and natives of the countries comprehended therein, and also build any forts and fortifications there, to appoint and discharge Governors, people for war, and officers of justice, and other public officers, for the preservation of the places, keeping good order, police and justice, and in like manner for the promoting of trade.

changes.text: Their [the English traders'] business in India cannot be managed without frequent gifts and presents to the rajas and governors, according to the practice in all the eastern countries. Forts and castles, with good garrisons, are there indispensably necessary for the preservation of the pepper-trade, and indeed needful upon many other accounts, … besides, they are a safety to our people from any insults of the natives, and a refuge upon any disorder, revolution, or other emergency in the Mogul's state and empire. … The Hollanders, at this time, are very powerful in India; they have many good forts and castles well provided, and large colonies of men; and they can, upon any occasion, call together there 40 strong frigates.

decisions.note: Compared with Avalon's text. 'Their' had no referent (in the source it refers back to 'the undertakers' who send large ships to India, i.e. the English traders), so a clarifying bracket was added. The first '…' marked only a paragraph break, so it was removed. The other cuts drop 'and magazines for naval provision...' (20 words) and ~1,400 words of profit figures before the passage on Dutch strength in India. Neither changes the meaning. The excerpt ends at a semicolon where the source goes on to say the Dutch could expel the English, which is consistent. 'written in defence of the East India Company' fits the essay, which argues against the bill banning East India silks and calicoes.

changes.sourceLine: Charles Davenant, English writer on trade and public finance and former commissioner of the excise, An Essay on the East-India Trade, 1697 (adapted)
changes.text: There is no trade so advantageous, especially to an island, as that of buying goods in one country, to sell them in another; and it is the original and chief article of the great wealth in Holland. There is gain by the freight; it occasions consumption of our home product; it breeds seamen, increases shipping, and improves navigation. … Our plantations (if we take care to preserve them from foreign insults and invasions) as they increase in people, will consume more of our home manufactures than we have hands to make: they produce commodities indispensably necessary to this part of the world, and not to be produced elsewhere, and, with industry and conduct, may be made an inexhaustible mine of treasure to their mother kingdom.

"[sic]" would have pinned it on Davenant, so the document is now adapted: "original" keeps the Avalon wording, "text" has the printed "inexhaustible" (no [sic]); every other word of the excerpt matches p. 36 of the 1696 printing. changes.sourceLine: Montesquieu (Charles de Secondat), French nobleman, former magistrate in the Parlement of Bordeaux, and political philosopher, The Spirit of Laws, book 21, chapter 21, on European colonies, 1748
changes.translation: Translated by Thomas Nugent (1750), revised by J. V. Prichard; The Spirit of Laws, G. Bell & Sons, London, 1914 (as reproduced by the Constitution Society)
changes.text: The colonies they [the nations of Europe] have formed are under a kind of dependence, of which there are but very few instances in all the colonies of the ancients; whether we consider them as holdings of the state itself, or of some trading company established in the state. The design of these colonies is to trade on more advantageous conditions than could otherwise be done with the neighbouring people, with whom all advantages are reciprocal. … Thus it is still a fundamental law of Europe that all commerce with a foreign colony shall be regarded as a mere monopoly, punishable by the laws of the country. … The disadvantage of a colony that loses the liberty of commerce is visibly compensated by the protection of the mother country, who defends it by her arms, or supports it by her laws.

decisions.note: Compared with constitution.org book 21, chapter 21 ('The Discovery of two new Worlds, and in what manner Europe is affected by it'). Words match. 'they' referred back to 'several nations' of Europe in the previous paragraph, so a clarifying bracket was added. The cuts (45 words: 'It has been established that the metropolis... alone shall trade in the colonies...'; 56 words on ancient precedent) do not change the meaning. Translation credit corrected to the 1914 G. Bell edition the site names, and role refined, as for the other Montesquieu document.

Compared with Gutenberg #75962 (Magoffin translation, ed. James Brown Scott, Oxford University Press for the Carnegie Endowment, 1916). The first piece is the opening of chapter I and the second the opening of chapter XIII ('The Dutch must maintain their right of trade with the East Indies by peace, by treaty, or by war'), both verbatim. The long cut joins Grotius's thesis to his conclusion and does not distort it. Mare Liberum was published in 1609; the Latin title page reproduced in the edition says 1608, the year it was written as part of his brief for the VOC, so year 1609 is right.

changes.text: Most humbly representing unto Your Majesty the inevitable destruction of those Colonies, if so be that the late Act for increase of Trade and Shipping [the Navigation Act] be not as to them dispensed with … Why these men [the Act's promoters] procured this Act, prohibiting the Hollanders trade into those Colonies at first, and its continuance now, was, and is, because they would keep still in their own hands that Trade which they had engrossed, and have no body come there to hinder them, and that for the following reasons. First, That for whatever goods they carried out of England to those Plantations, the Inhabitants should pay to them what prices and rates they pleased to require, else they should have nothing at all of them to supply their necessities. Secondly, To force the Planters to deliver them such Tobaccoes, which by the labour and sweat of their brows they had made, at the rates they themselves trading thither would have it, whereby they got that oftentimes of the poor Planters for a halfpenny, which they made us pay for here in England by Retale three or four shillings.

decisions.note: Compared with the EarlyPrint text A28354 and with the EEBO-TCP original-spelling transcription (Wing B3157, ESTC R33225; '[London?, 1661?]', 'Place and date of publication suggested by Wing'), so 'c. 1661' is right. EarlyPrint only standardises spelling (encrease→increase, dispenc'd→dispensed, Majesties→Majesty's, browes→brows, ingrossed→engrossed). The words match the TCP text. The bracket '[The Act's promoters intended:]' stood in for a cut sentence, so it was replaced by restoring the source sentence: 'Why these men procured this Act... was, and is, because they would keep still in their own hands that Trade which they had engrossed... for the following reasons.' 'these men' gets a referent bracket using the source's own word 'promoters'. To stay under 200 words, the clause 'for it will not only ruinate the Inhabitants and Planters, but make desolate ... Dominion' after 'dispensed with' is now cut (marked …). The petition's claim of 'inevitable destruction of those Colonies' stays.

changes.text: What obstructions do you find to the improvement of the trade and navigation of the plantations within your government? Answer. Mighty and destructive, by that severe act of parliament, which excludes us the having any commerce with any nation in Europe but our own, so that we cannot add to our plantation any commodity that grows out of it. … for it is not lawful for us to carry a pipe stave, or a barrel of corn to any place in Europe out of the king's dominions. If this were for his majesty's service or the good of his subjects, we should not repine, whatever our sufferings are for it; but on my soul, it is the contrary for both. And this is the cause why no small or great vessels are built here; for we are most obedient to all laws, whilst the New England men break through, and men trade to any place that their interest lead them.

decisions.note: Compared with Hening, Statutes at Large vol. 2, pp. 515–516 (page images viewed, leaves 533–534). Hening introduces the 'Enquiries to the Governor of Virginia' as 'propounded in the year 1670, and received their answers in 1671, while Sir William Berkeley was governor', so the attribution and 1671 are right. The printed word is 'com-' + 'merce' across the page break; the OCR has 'com- … mei'ce' with side-notes between. The text had '[commerce]' in brackets as if it were an editorial insertion. It is now plain 'commerce' (an OCR correction confirmed on the image). The rest of the word diff is spelling only (lawfull→lawful, vessells→vessels) and matches the image, including 'and men trade to any place that their interest lead them'. The cut ('as olive trees, cotton or vines. Besides this, ... silk;') keeps the meaning.

Compared with Murdoch, History of Japan [During the Century of Early Foreign Intercourse 1542-1651], Kobe 1903 (archive.org historyofjapan02murd, catalogued as vol. 2), p. 243: text is continuous and verbatim; Murdoch introduces it as the Edict 'published and posted up in Hakata' on 25 July 1587. The version is the one given by the Jesuit historians (Murdoch cites Charlevoix/Crasset in the same passage), so the credit's 'from a European version of the edict' is accurate. Hideyoshi was kampaku (imperial regent) in 1587. 1450-1750 primary source; reads on its own.

Compared with Murdoch 1903, pp. 375-376 ('To the Viceroy of the Indies the Regent wrote as follows', dated 1591 by Murdoch). Words verbatim; the one cut removes the Confucian-order sentence ('the good order of the government ... tranquillity abroad'), which does not alter the religious argument; excerpt ends at 'in all security' where the source has a semicolon. Murdoch gives no source for this version; credit says honestly it comes from a European version. Year 1591 matches.

changes.sourceLine: Senior councillors of the Tokugawa shogunate, sentence signed at Edo and read at Nagasaki to the envoys sent from Portuguese Macao to ask for the reopening of trade, 1640
changes.translation: Translated in James Murdoch and Isoh Yamagata, A History of Japan, vol. 2, 1903 (from the European accounts of the episode by the Jesuit Cardim and others, not the Japanese original)
changes.text: The crimes committed by these men during a long series of years in promulgating the Christian faith contrary to the decrees of the Shogun are very numerous, and exceedingly serious; last year [1639] the Shogun has, under the gravest penalties, forbidden any one to sail from Macao to Japan, and he has decreed that in case any vessel disregard this prohibition, the said vessel shall be burned, and all her crew and passengers put to death without exception. … It is decreed that the vessel shall be burned, and that the chiefs of the embassy with all their suite shall be put to death, in order that the bruit of this example may reach Macao and even the country of Europe … We mean, however, that the lowest among the crew be spared and sent back to Macao. If by any chance whatsoever — from stress of weather or from any other cause — any Portuguese vessel put into a Japanese harbour, no matter where, all on board of her shall be put to death to the last man.

decisions.note: Compared with Murdoch 1903, pp. 665-667. Attribution: Murdoch says the sentence was 'drawn up and signed by all the senior members of the Shogun's Government on July 21st' in Edo and read by an interpreter at Nagasaki at the commissioners' order (Aug. 1640), so sourceLine changed from 'Commissioners of the Tokugawa shogunate'. Translation: Murdoch's footnote 1 p. 665 names the 'chief original authorities' as Father Cardim (Jesuit, Macao) and the Spaniard Magisu, used by Charlevoix and Pages, so the credit now says it is from European accounts, not the Japanese text. '[1639]' is Murdoch's own bracket (OCR '[1639J'). (p. 667), leaving 'all her crew ... put to death without exception' unqualified; restored it from the page (174 words).

changes.sourceLine: Engelbert Kaempfer, German physician with the Dutch embassy to the shogun Tokugawa Tsunayoshi at Edo in 1691, The History of Japan (written after his return to Europe, published in English 1727)
changes.text: As for my own particular the following questions were put to me: What external and internal distempers I thought the most dangerous, and most difficult to cure? How I proceeded in the cure of cancrous humors and imposthumations of the inner parts? Whether our European Physicians did not search after some Medicine to render people immortal, as the Chinese Physicians had done for many hundred years? Whether we had made any considerable progress in this search, and which was the last remedy conducive to long life, that had been found out in Europe? … Then ’twas ask’d, whether it [the remedy] could be had at Batavia? and having return’d in answer, that it was to be had there, the Emperor [the shogun] desir’d, that it should be sent over by the next ships.

decisions.note: Compared with Kaempfer, History of Japan (Scheuchzer trans., Glasgow 1906), vol. III, pp. 91-92 (margin 'A.D. 1691'): pieces verbatim; '[the shogun]' glosses Kaempfer's 'Emperor'. The 239-word cut removes the naming of the medicine (Sal volatile Oleosum Sylvii), leaving 'whether it could be had' without a clear referent: added the clarifying bracket 'it [the remedy]'. sourceLine 'written in the 1690s' changed to 'written after his return to Europe' (as for kaempfer-1692-dejima). Year 1691 = audience at Edo (margin date). Lead verifier: added "in 1691" after "at Edo" so the sourceLine shows the date that "year" gives (the margin date of the audience).

changes.sourceLine: Xu Guangqi, Ming scholar-official, mathematician and Christian convert, memorial to the Wanli emperor defending the Jesuits accused by the Board of Rites, 1616
changes.translation: Translator not named; English version printed in The Chinese Repository, March 1850, as modernised by Jerome S. Arkenberg (Internet Modern History Sourcebook)
changes.text: Knowing full well that the arts and sciences of the foreigners are in a high degree correct, your majesty's humble servant earnestly begs of his sacred Intelligence, the illustrious honor of issuing a manifesto in their behalf, so as to render his own felicity eternal, and give great tranquility to ten thousand generations. … As your servant for years past has been thus accustomed to engage in discussions and investigations with these courtiers [the Jesuit missionaries], he has become well acquainted with them, and knows that they are not only in deportment and in heart wholly free from aught which can excite suspicion, but that they are indeed worthies and sages; that their doctrines are most correct; their regimen most strict; their learning most extensive; their knowledge most refined; their hearts most true; their views most steady; and that among the people of their own nations, there is not one in a thousand so accomplished, or one in ten thousand so talented as these men.

decisions.note: Fordham 1617hsukuang.asp ('Memorial to Fra Matteo Ricci, 1617'; source note: Chinese Repository, March 1850, pp. 118-126, modernised by Arkenberg; no translator named, so credit made explicit). Pieces verbatim; cut removes the Board of Rites report and Xu's own involvement, meaning intact. Added '[the Jesuit missionaries]' after 'these courtiers' (no referent for 'courtiers' in the excerpt). Date: the memorial answers the 1616 accusations by Shen Que of the (Nanjing) Board of Rites; it is Xu's 'Bianxue zhangshu' of Wanli 44 = 1616 (zh.wikipedia 'Nanjing jiao'an' dates the incident and Xu's memorial, quoting this very passage, to 1616; Pantoja was expelled at the end of that year). The Sourcebook's '1617' is the later date; year and sourceLine set to 1616 (id left unchanged).

changes.sourceLine: Xu Guangqi, Ming scholar-official and Christian convert, memorial to the Wanli emperor proposing how the Jesuits should be examined, 1616
changes.translation: Translator not named; English version printed in The Chinese Repository, March 1850, as modernised by Jerome S. Arkenberg (Internet Modern History Sourcebook)
changes.text: 1st. Let all the courtiers [the Jesuit missionaries], whose names have been included in the memorials, be called to the capital; and let a selection be made of your majesty's ministers both in and out of the capital; let all these jointly translate the standard works that have been brought from the West; let subjects be taken up in detail—what is said on serving Heaven and loving man, what relates to natural and moral philosophy, to the systems of civil government, to astronomy, to mathematics, to physic and medicine, to agriculture and irrigation, to political economy, &c.; and let a distinct treatise be prepared on each of these; and then let his majesty command the ministers of his own palace, in general assembly, to decide whether they are correct or erroneous. And if indeed they be subversive of the cardinal virtues and opposed to the classics, involving wicked doctrines and sinister means, then let the said courtiers be immediately dismissed and expelled; and your majesty's servant will willingly abide the punishment appointed for those who aid and abet the deceivers of his majesty.

Added '[the Jesuit missionaries]' after 'the courtiers' for a student reading it alone. Date corrected to 1616 and translation credit made explicit, as for xu-guangqi-1617-defends-jesuit-learning (same memorial).

changes.sourceLine: Francisco Hernández Arana Xajilá, Kaqchikel Maya noble who lived through the Spanish conquest (Brinton's edition credits this early part to his father), The Annals of the Cakchiquels (written c. 1560s–1580s), on the Kaqchikel revolt of 1524
changes.text: Then Tunatiuh [Pedro de Alvarado] began to ask the chiefs for money. He wished that they should give him jars full of precious metals, and even their drinking cups and crowns. Not receiving anything, Tunatiuh became angry and said to the chiefs: “Why have you not given me the metal? If you do not bring me the precious metal in all your towns, choose then, for I shall burn you alive and hang you.” Thus did he speak to the chiefs. … Thus it was that our city was abandoned on the day 7 Ahmak on account of a priest of the Demon, O my children. … But what the chiefs did was soon known to Tunatiuh. Ten days after we had left the city, war was begun by Tunatiuh. On the day 4 Camey began our destruction. Then began our misery. We scattered in the forests; all our towns were taken, O my children; we were slaughtered by Tunatiuh. The Castilians entered the city and they arrived as to a deserted spot. From that time the Castilians were hated by the Cakchiquels. They made trenches, they dug pitfalls, that the horses might be killed, and war was waged by their men.

decisions.note: Compared with Brinton, The Annals of the Cakchiquels (Philadelphia, 1885), §§152 and 156 (English). Text matches; the cut (§§153–155: more gold demands, the chiefs' payment and their flight from Iximche on a priest's advice) is marked, and '[abandoning their capital, Iximche]' is a pure insertion clarifying 'what the chiefs did' (it summarises §155, which says the city of Iximche was deserted); '[Pedro de Alvarado]' glosses Tunatiuh. Attribution: Brinton's introduction (pp. 57–58) says the writer first names himself as Francisco Ernantez Arana in 1582, but argues the part up to 1559 (which includes 1524) was written by his father, an adult at the conquest, and that Francisco continued it 1560–1583; the sourceLine now says so rather than giving one author as settled. Year 1575 kept as an estimate for a text compiled between c. 1559 and 1583 (Brinton's dates). Lead verifier override: the bracket "[abandoning their capital, Iximche]" summarised the cut §155 rather than naming a referent, so it is removed and the last sentence of §155 is restored from the page instead ("Thus it was that our city was abandoned on the day 7 Ahmak on account of a priest of the Demon, O my children."); "But what the chiefs did was soon known to Tunatiuh" (§156) follows; the "…" between them spans only the Kaqchikel-language text of §156 and the section number on the bilingual page, no English words. Now 197 words.

changes.sourceLine: Powhatan (Wahunsenacah), paramount chief of the Powhatan peoples of Virginia, speech to John Smith in 1609, as recorded by Smith's companions (this section by Anas Todkill) in The Proceedings of the English Colonie in Virginia, 1612 (adapted)
changes.translation: Powhatan's words as rendered in English by the colonists (no interpreter named); The Proceedings of the English Colonie in Virginia, Oxford, 1612, reprinted in Travels and Works of Captain John Smith, ed. Edward Arber, new ed. A. G. Bradley, 1910
changes.text: What will it avail you to take that perforce, you may quietly have with love, or to destroy them that provide you food? What can you get by war, when we can hide our provision and fly to the woods, whereby you must famish, by wronging us your friends? And why are you thus jealous of our loves, seeing us unarmed, and both do, and are willing still to feed you with that you cannot get but by our labours? Think you I am so simple not to know it is better to eat good meat, lie well, and sleep quietly with my women and children, laugh and be merry with you, have copper, hatchets, or what I want, being your friend; than be forced to fly from all, to lie cold in the woods, feed upon acorns, roots and such trash, and be so hunted by you that I can neither rest, eat nor sleep …
changes.original: What will it availe you to take that perforce, you may quietly haue with loue, or to destroy them that provide you food ? What can you get by war, when we can hide our provision and flie to the woodes, whereby you must famish, by wronging vs your friends ? And whie are you thus iealous of our loues, seeing vs vnarmed, and both doe, and are willing still to feed you with that you cannot get but by our labours ? Think you I am so simple not to knowe it is better to eate good meate, lie well, and sleepe quietly with my women and children, laugh and be merrie with you, haue copper, hatchets, or what I want, being your friend ; then bee forced to flie from al, to lie cold in the woods, feed vpon acorns roots and such trash, and be so hunted by you that I can neither rest eat nor sleepe …

changes.text: Thirdly: "What do these souls do when they arrive at their dwelling place?" "During the daytime, they are seated with their two elbows upon their two knees, and their heads between their two hands, the usual position of sick Savages; during the night, they go and come, they work, they go to the chase." "Oh, but they cannot see at all during the night," I rejoined. "Thou art an ignoramus, thou hast no sense," they answered; "souls are not like us, they do not see at all during the day, and see very clearly at night; their day is in the darkness of the night, and their night in the light of the day." … And when they see that I make sport of their dreams, they are astonished and ask me, "What does thou believe then, if thou dost not believe in thy dream?" "I believe in him who has made all things, and who can do all things." "Thou hast no sense, how canst thou believe in him, if thou hast not seen him?"

changes.text: On the 17th December, 1637, we received intelligence that the peasants in the county of Arima had revolted, taken up arms, set fire to all the habitations of the nobility and citizens, murdered some of the nobles … The newly-arrived lord [Matsukura, Bungo-no-Kami], not content herewith, imposed moreover upon them [the former lord's retainers, now farmers] and upon the other farmers more taxes, and forced them to raise such a quantity of rice as was impossible for them to do. Those who could not pay the fixed taxes were dressed, by his order, in a rough straw coat (mino) … These mantles were tied round the neck and body, the hands being tightly bound behind their backs with ropes, after which the straw-coats were set on fire. … but as his son, the present lord [Matsukura, Nagato-no-Kami], who resides in Yedo, feels also inclined to follow in the footsteps of his father, and forces the farmers to pay far more taxes than they are able to do, in such a manner that they languish from hunger … the people resolved not to bear any longer the vexations, and to die one single death instead of the many slow deaths to which they were subjected.

decisions.note: Compared with Murdoch 1903, pp. 650-651 ('Koeckebacker's letter to Governor-General Van Diemen'). The old final cut jumped from the father's straw-coat torture to 'the people resolved...', but the source says the people endured the newly-arrived lord's cruelty 'as long as he was present' and rose because his son, the present lord, kept overtaxing them. That changed the cause, so the son's clause was restored from the page ('but as his son, the present lord [Matsukura, Nagato-no-Kami] ... they languish from hunger'; the bracket is Murdoch's). To stay under 200 words the description of the mino grass was cut, and so was 'taking ouly some roots...' (OCR error). Added clarifying brackets '[Matsukura, Bungo-no-Kami]' (from Murdoch's n.3) and 'them [the former lord's retainers, now farmers]', whose referent was in the cut paragraph. Now 190 words, every piece at least 27 words. No translator named on the page, so the credit says so.

changes.text: In the second place, it is clear that the peasants demand that this Gospel be taught them as a guide in life, and they ought not to be called disobedient or disorderly. … First, it is our humble petition and desire, as also our will and resolution, that in the future we should have power and authority so that each community should choose and appoint a pastor, and that we should have the right to depose him should he conduct himself improperly. The pastor thus chosen should teach us the Gospel pure and simple, without any addition, doctrine or ordinance of man. … We will that for the future our church provost, whomsoever the community may appoint, shall gather and receive this tithe. From this he shall give to the pastor, elected by the whole community, a decent and sufficient maintenance for him …

changes.text: It has been the custom hitherto for men to hold us as their own property, which is pitiable enough, considering that Christ has delivered and redeemed us all, without exception, by the shedding of his precious blood, the lowly as well as the great. Accordingly, it is consistent with Scripture that we should be free and wish to be so. Not that we would wish to be absolutely free and under no authority. … We are thus ready to yield obedience according to God's law to our elected and regular authorities in all proper things becoming to a Christian. We, therefore, take it for granted that you will release us from serfdom, as true Christians, unless it should be shown us from the Gospel that we are serfs. … In the eighth place, we are greatly burdened by holdings which cannot support the rent exacted from them. The peasants suffer loss in this way and are ruined; and we ask that the lords may appoint persons of honor to inspect these holdings, and fix a rent in accordance with justice, so that the peasant shall not work for nothing, since the laborer is worthy of his hire.
changes.translation: Translated by the editors, James Harvey Robinson and Merrick Whitcomb, in Translations and Reprints from the Original Sources of European History, vol. 2, no. 6 (Period of the Early Reformation in Germany), University of Pennsylvania Press; this printing undated

decisions.note: Compared with Translations and Reprints vol. 2 no. 6, pp. 27-29 (Third and Eighth Articles). changes.text: The root of all this mischief we find to be a malignant and pernicious design of subverting the fundamental laws and principles of government, upon which the religion and justice of this kingdom are firmly established. The actors and promoters hereof have been: 1. The Jesuited Papists, who hate the laws, as the obstacles of that change and subversion of religion which they so much long for. 2. The Bishops, and the corrupt part of the Clergy, who cherish formality and superstition as the natural effects and more probable supports of their own ecclesiastical tyranny and usurpation. … And although all this [Tonnage and Poundage and other customs duties] was taken upon pretence of guarding the seas, yet a new unheard-of tax of ship-money was devised, and upon the same pretence, by both which there was charged upon the subject near £700,000 some years, and yet the merchants have been left so naked to the violence of the Turkish pirates, that many great ships of value and thousands of His Majesty's subjects have been taken by them, and do still remain in miserable slavery.

decisions.note: Compared with constitution.org, Gardiner, Constitutional Documents of the Puritan Revolution, no. 43 ('Presented to the King, December 1, 1641'). changes.text: Emeri, Superintendent of the Finances, and in my opinion the most corrupt man of the age, multiplied edicts as fast as he could find names to call them by. … In August, 1647, there was a mighty clamour against the tariff edict imposing a general tax upon all provisions that came into Paris, which the people were resolved to bear no longer. But the gentlemen of the Council being determined to support it, the Queen consulted the members deputed from Parliament, when Cardinal Mazarin, a mere ignoramus in these affairs, said he wondered that so considerable a body as they were should mind such trifles,—an expression truly worthy of Mazarin. However, the Council at length imagining the Parliament would do it, thought fit to suppress the tariff themselves by a declaration, in order to save the King’s credit. … Thereupon they [the Council] trumped up a declaration which had been registered two years before for the establishment of the Chamber of Domain, which was a terrible charge upon the people … The people mutinied, went in crowds to the Palace, and used very abusive language to the President de Thore, Emeri’s son.
changes.translation: Anonymous English translation, 1723; Project Gutenberg text (Historic Court Memoirs series), whose wording matches the 1896 London reprint by H. S. Nichols, “reprinted from a translation dated 1723”

decisions.note: Compared with the Gutenberg text (Book II) and the 1896 H. S. Nichols edition (archive.org cu31924028186421, pp. 71-72), whose wording matches. The last cut skipped the Council's five new edicts and its revival of the Chamber of Domain declaration, so 'The people mutinied…' read as a reaction to the suppressed tariff; in the source the mutiny follows the Chamber of Domain declaration, 'a terrible charge upon the people'. Restored that clause from the page ('Thereupon they [the Council] trumped up a declaration… a terrible charge upon the people'; bracket only names the referent of 'they'); 187 words. Translation: the Gutenberg page names no translator or edition; the 1896 Nichols reprint's publisher's note says it 'is reprinted from a translation dated 1723' and its text matches the excerpt word for word, but the Gutenberg file (Historic Court Memoirs series) is not that 1896 printing (its preface modernises names, e.g. 'Philippe' for 'Philip'), so the credit was reworded. changes.text: On the 26th of August, 1648, the worthy Broussel, councillor of the Grand Chamber, and Rene Potier, Sieur de Blancmenil, President of the Inquests, were both arrested by the Queen’s officers. … The Chancellor, hemmed in on every side, narrowly escaped with his life to the Hotel d’O, which the people broke open, rushed in with fury … The news of this occurrence ran like wild-fire through the whole city. Men and women were immediately up in arms, and mothers even put daggers into the hands of their children. In less than two hours there were erected above two hundred barricades, adorned with all the standards and colours that the League had left entire. All the cry was, “God bless the King!” sometimes, “God bless the Coadjutor!” and the echo was, “No Mazarin!” … The Court minions of the two last centuries knew not what they did when they reduced that effectual regard which kings ought to have for their subjects into mere style and form; for there are, as you see, certain conjunctures in which, by a necessary consequence, subjects make a mere form also of the real obedience which they owe to their sovereigns.
changes.translation: Anonymous English translation, 1723; Project Gutenberg text (Historic Court Memoirs series), whose wording matches the 1896 London reprint by H. S. Nichols, “reprinted from a translation dated 1723”

Translation credit corrected as for retz-1647 (1723 anonymous translation; Gutenberg text matches the 1896 Nichols reprint 'from a translation dated 1723'). changes.sourceLine: Niccolao Manucci, Venetian who lived in India from 1653 and served Mughal princes as gunner and physician, Storia do Mogor, Part IV (written after August 1702), on the poll tax (jizya) imposed on Hindus in 1679
changes.text: It was during the years 1678 and 1679 that Aurangzeb decided to impose a new tribute upon all the Hindus. … But all was in vain, and the king stood firm, still more so because it was his purpose to spread the Mahomedan religion among those people (the Hindus). He was of the opinion that he had found in this tax an excellent means of succeeding in converting them, besides … thereby replenishing his treasuries greatly, which were daily becoming depleted. … Begam Sahib, eldest sister of the king, a very generous princess, wanted to make a fresh appeal. With this intent she paid her brother a visit, and entreated most humbly that he would not go farther with this affair … ‘Just think, sire,’ said she, ‘that the lands of Hindustan are like a vast ocean; your majesty and all the other members of our royal family are like ships navigating its waters and ploughing through its waves. Where is there any sovereign prince who would desire to load with imposts the sea on which he sails? Who has ever seen the physician pay the patient?’

changes.text: As it is apparent to all that a prince is constituted by God to be ruler of a people, to defend them from oppression and violence as the shepherd his sheep; and whereas God did not create the people slaves to their prince, to obey his commands, whether right or wrong, but rather the prince for the sake of the subjects (without which he could be no prince), to govern them according to equity, to love and support them as a father his children or a shepherd his flock, and even at the hazard of life to defend and preserve them. And when he does not behave thus, but, on the contrary, oppresses them, seeking opportunities to infringe their ancient customs and privileges, exacting from them slavish compliance, then he is no longer a prince, but a tyrant, and the subjects are to consider him in no other view. And particularly when this is done deliberately, unauthorized by the states, they may not only disallow his authority, but legally proceed to the choice of another prince for their defense.

changes.sourceLine: Articles of Pacification concluded by John Guthrie and Francis Sadler for the British colonial government of Jamaica with the Maroons of Trelawny Town led by Captain Cudjoe, 1 March 1739 (dated 1738, Old Style), as printed in R. changes.text: Whereas Captain Cudjoe, Captain Acompong, Captain Johnny, Captain Cuffee, Captain Quaco, and several other negroes, their dependants and adherents, have been in a state of war and hostility, for several years past, against our sovereign Lord the King, and the inhabitants of this island; … First, That all hostilities shall cease on both sides for ever. Second, That the said Captain Cudjoe, the rest of his captains, adherents, and men, shall be for ever hereafter in a perfect state of freedom and liberty, … Third, That they shall enjoy and possess, for themselves and posterity for ever, all the lands situate and lying between Trelawny Town and the Cockpits, to the amount of fifteen hundred acres, bearing north-west from the said Trelawny Town. … Ninth, That if any negroes shall hereafter run away from their masters or owners, and fall into Captain Cudjoe’s hands, they shall immediately be sent back to the chief magistrate of the next parish where they are taken; and those that bring them are to be satisfied for their trouble, as the legislature shall appoint.
